title: Intel Server CPU Share for Advanced Processes
gist: A Mercury Research-sourced Q2 2026 CPU report shows AMD hitting record x86 unit share as desktop shipments crater 20% and Intel floods the laptop market, prompting a forum question about which of Intel or AMD actually leads server CPU share on sub-7nm process nodes released within the last five years.

insights.claim: In Q2 2026, overall x86 CPU unit shipments grew 10% sequentially, as growth in data center and laptop processor shipments more than offset declining desktop CPU sales and lower-end embedded/IoT product sales, according to a Mercury Research report.
insights.speaker: Xebec
insights.so_what: The CPU market's growth engine has shifted to data center and laptop segments while desktop keeps shrinking, so investors should weight PC-supply-chain exposure toward enterprise/laptop mix over consumer desktop.
insights.quote: The second quarter of 2026 was quite favorable for CPU suppliers, as unit growth was 10% sequentially, with data center and laptop processor shipments more than offsetting declining sales of desktop CPUs and lower-end products for embedded and IoT applications, according to a new report by Mercury Research.

insights.claim: Desktop x86 CPU shipments fell 20% amid high component costs, leading Tom's Hardware to characterize the desktop processor market as 'ugly.'
insights.speaker: Xebec
insights.so_what: A 20% desktop unit decline signals weak consumer PC replacement demand, a headwind for desktop-exposed component suppliers such as motherboard, PSU and discrete-GPU makers.
insights.quote: Desktop CPU shipments crater 20% amid high component costs, but AMD gains record share despite 'ugly' desktop processor market
insights.locator: quoted headline near top of thread

insights.claim: AMD continued to gain x86 CPU market share in Q2 2026, with its unit shipments and share reaching a new all-time record despite the weak desktop market.
insights.speaker: Xebec
insights.so_what: AMD's share record occurring even inside a shrinking desktop segment implies genuine competitive displacement of Intel rather than just riding overall market growth.
insights.quote: AMD continued to gain market share, so its unit shipments and share reached a new record during the quarter

insights.claim: Intel managed to increase shipments of its client and data center CPUs during the quarter and flooded the laptop market with millions of units.
insights.speaker: Xebec
insights.so_what: Intel's laptop volume push suggests it is prioritizing unit share and OEM presence in laptops even as it loses ground in desktop and faces node-based competition from AMD in servers.
insights.quote: Intel floods laptop market with millions of CPUs
insights.locator: quoted headline near top of thread

insights.claim: Apple sold a large volume of processors through its popular MacBook Neo laptops during the quarter, called out alongside AMD and Intel in the same shipment report.
insights.speaker: Xebec
insights.so_what: Apple Silicon's laptop volumes are now large enough to be benchmarked against Intel and AMD in the same industry report, underscoring Apple's growing footprint in a market still framed around x86 competition.
insights.quote: Apple sold a boatload of processors in its popular MacBook Neo laptops

themes.theme: Framing the leading-edge server CPU share question

insights.claim: After reviewing 10-Q filings and estimated TSMC wafer loadings, the poster raises an open question: which of Intel or AMD actually sells the most server CPU chips built on processes below 7nm (Intel's 18A or Intel 3 nodes versus AMD's TSMC N5/N4, N3, or N2 nodes)?
insights.speaker: Xebec
insights.so_what: Reframes the Intel-vs-AMD server rivalry around leading-edge process-node unit share rather than headline market share, which is the more relevant lens for margin and AI-server competitiveness.
insights.quote: Which company, Intel or AMD, sells the most Server CPU Chips below 7nm (Intel 18A or 3, AMD N5/N4, N3, N2)?

insights.claim: The poster further narrows the comparison to only count process nodes originally released within the last five years, as a way to isolate leadership in genuinely modern server silicon rather than legacy-node volume.
insights.speaker: Xebec
insights.so_what: A five-year-node cutoff is a useful heuristic for separating 'modern, fab-competitive' share from stale-node volume that can inflate headline market-share figures.
insights.quote: Who has highest market share if we only include processes originally released in the last 5 years?
